title: Joel 1:13–20
context: Joel now calls the priests to put on sackcloth and lead a fast and solemn assembly at the house of the LORD (1:13–14), because the daily offerings have ceased. In 1:15 he announces that “the day of the LORD is at hand,” the first mention of a theme that runs through the book; the locust disaster is read as a foretaste or herald of that day. The land’s ruin is described in seed, granary, and barn, and in the groaning of livestock (1:16–18). The unit ends with Joel’s own prayer (1:19–20): “LORD, I cry to you,” joined by the animals that pant toward God. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a model of communal lament that turns disaster into prayer, and they see the day of the LORD here as near judgment that also points beyond itself.

verses.text: Put on sackcloth and mourn, you priests! Wail, you ministers of the altar. Come, lie all night in sackcloth, you ministers of my God, for the meal offering and the drink offering are withheld from your God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel calls the priests to put on sackcloth, mourn, and lie all night in sackcloth, since offerings are withheld. Arminian readers see the priests called to lead the people in humble repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the priests’ role as intercessors brought to the fore in a time of crisis. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the religious leaders modeling lament before the whole community.

verses.text: Sanctify a fast. Call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to the house of the LORD, your God, and cry to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests are to sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather everyone to the LORD’s house, and cry out. Arminian readers see a community turning together to God, seeking mercy through prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as the proper response to judgment, a gathering before God in dependence. Both traditions read the verse as a model of corporate prayer and fasting in times of national distress.

verses.text: Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is at hand, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel cries, Alas for the day, for the day of the LORD is at hand, coming as destruction from the Almighty. Arminian readers see the locust plague as a warning that a greater day of judgment draws near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the plague as a foretaste of the day of the LORD, compare Isaiah 13:6 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the day of the LORD in historical, typological, and future ways, and they share the sense of urgency.

verses.text: Isn’t the food cut off before our eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?
verses.arminianNotes: Joel asks whether food and joy are not cut off before their eyes from God’s house. Arminian readers see the people invited to recognize what they themselves have witnessed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loss at the house of God as the most painful sign of judgment. Both traditions read the question as pointing to visible, undeniable loss in both daily life and worship.

verses.text: The seeds rot under their clods. The granaries are laid desolate. The barns are broken down, for the grain has withered.
verses.arminianNotes: Seeds rot under clods, granaries lie desolate, and barns are broken, for the grain has withered. Arminian readers see the failure of future harvests as well as present ones, compounding the crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse showing how completely the land’s productivity has collapsed. Shared ground: both traditions read the detail as realistic description of agricultural disaster, which may have been worsened by drought.

verses.text: How the animals groan! The herds of livestock are perplexed, because they have no pasture. Yes, the flocks of sheep are made desolate.
verses.arminianNotes: The animals groan and the herds are perplexed, for they have no pasture. Arminian readers see creation sharing in the suffering, as even livestock feel the effects of the disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Scripture often depicts animals as sharing in human judgment and blessing, compare Romans 8:22 by reference. Both traditions read the groaning animals as a moving picture of a whole land in distress.

verses.text: LORD, I cry to you, for the fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and the flame has burned all the trees of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel prays, LORD, I cry to you, for fire has devoured the pastures and burned the trees. Arminian readers see the prophet modeling the prayer he has called for, bringing the crisis directly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet as intercessor, taking the people’s plight to the only one who can help. Shared ground: both traditions read the prayer as personal and heartfelt, an example of turning lament into petition.

verses.text: Yes, the animals of the field pant to you, for the water brooks have dried up, and the fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The animals of the field pant to God, for the brooks are dry and fire has devoured the pastures. Arminian readers see creation itself joining the prophet’s cry, as if the beasts too look to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the provider for all creatures, compare Psalm 104:27 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as closing the chapter with creation and prophet together crying out to the LORD.
